assessment.nobel_worthiness: Transformative measurement and analysis of long-run inequality, bringing distributional evidence to central economic and public debate.
assessment.attribution: Piketty, Saez and Zucman form a coherent core spanning historical income and wealth series, top-income measurement, and offshore wealth.
assessment.maturity: The research agenda has accumulated extensive data, replications, methodological debate and wide influence over more than two decades.
uncertainties: The appropriate division between foundational measurement and subsequent policy interpretation remains contestable.
Cross-country wealth and offshore-asset estimates necessarily involve substantial measurement assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established how technological change, trade shocks and task reallocation reshape local labour markets and wage inequality.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson provide a closely connected empirical and conceptual core, especially for task change and trade-shock evidence.
assessment.maturity: The findings have generated a large subsequent literature and remain central to understanding structural transformation.
uncertainties: Separating technology, trade and broader regional adjustment mechanisms is empirically difficult.
Credit is diffuse, including important related work on labour-market institutions and inequality.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative-data research has changed the measurement of intergenerational mobility and its geographic determinants.
assessment.attribution: Chetty, Hendren and Friedman are central to the linked data infrastructure and influential empirical research programme.
assessment.maturity: The work has been widely scrutinized, extended internationally and integrated into research and policy discussion.
uncertainties: Mobility estimates depend on cohort, income-definition and geographic-assignment choices.
The evidence identifies strong associations and local variation more securely than complete causal explanations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Clarified how agglomeration, cities and spatial sorting shape productivity, innovation, housing and regional inequality.
assessment.attribution: Glaeser, Puga and Moretti represent major complementary theoretical and empirical contributions to modern urban economics.
assessment.maturity: The framework is longstanding, extensively tested and highly consequential for research on regional growth and policy.
uncertainties: Housing, urban and spatial-equilibrium contributions involve several additional deserving researchers.
Causal attribution between place effects and sorting remains challenging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework supplied a powerful quantitative account of productivity gaps across firms and countries.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh, Klenow and Restuccia are leading architects of the theoretical and measurement-based research programme.
assessment.maturity: The approach has stimulated extensive application, refinement and debate in growth and development economics.
uncertainties: Measured dispersion can reflect adjustment costs, demand variation and measurement error as well as distortions.
The scale of aggregate productivity gains remains model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Audit and correspondence studies made discrimination measurable with transparent field-experimental designs and changed labour-market research.
assessment.attribution: Bertrand and Mullainathan are the clearest credited pair for the influential modern correspondence-study contribution.
assessment.maturity: The designs have been replicated widely across settings and have enduring methodological and social importance.
uncertainties: Experimental responses at the application stage need not identify all mechanisms or later-stage discrimination.
The broader audit-study tradition predates this particular contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political-economy research on institutions, state capacity, fiscal systems and electoral incentives has deepened understanding of long-run development and governance.
assessment.attribution: Besley, Persson and Tabellini have made distinct but mutually reinforcing foundational contributions.
assessment.maturity: The scholarship is well established and influential across political economy, public finance and development.
uncertainties: Institutional outcomes are difficult to identify causally and often depend on historical context.
Attribution overlaps with a broad earlier literature on political institutions and growth.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Their work placed exhaustible resources, natural capital and intergenerational welfare at the centre of economic analysis.
assessment.attribution: Dasgupta and Heal are a natural foundational pair for this line of environmental economic thought.
assessment.maturity: The theoretical work is longstanding and increasingly important for evaluating sustainability and inclusive wealth.
uncertainties: Valuing biodiversity and natural capital remains conceptually and empirically unsettled.
The contribution overlaps with a broad environmental-economics tradition.
